body: The guitarist counts them in and it falls apart in the second line. Thursday evening practice, a church hall in Delhi, the same eight bars for twenty minutes; he counts them in again, more slowly, and it falls apart in the same place. The tabla player is not making a mistake; he is landing his weight where his cycle tells him to land it, and the guitarist keeps hearing that as an early beat and pushing against it. Somebody suggests the tabla just play straight through. The tabla player, who is nineteen and has been doing this since he was seven, says he can, and does, and afterwards nobody says the arrangement is better and nobody says it is worse.

What went into the recording that week was a compromise nobody in the room would have chosen if they had been allowed to start from the other end. The song had already decided what the drums were for before the drummer arrived.

The cheap approach to Hindi worship is to take the Western song form — verse, chorus, bridge, four chords, a fixed harmonic destination — and put Hindi words on it. It is quick, it is singable by anybody who has heard Western pop, and it is what a great deal of the available material sounds like.

It is worth being exact about what that leaves out, because leaves out sounds like a matter of flavour and it is not. Indian classical and devotional music is organised around raga rather than around chord progression: melodic frameworks with their own rules about which notes may be approached from where, their own emotional associations, and in the classical system their own times of day. Rhythm is organised in cycles rather than in bars, with the weight falling at a point in the cycle rather than at the front of every group of four. Set a Hindi text over a Western chord progression and you have not localised anything. You have made a translation with a costume on.
So the station gets its own number rather than a slot. HM 332.10 — Inspire India — is the Hindi-language station, one of 40 international frequencies on a dial running from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70.

Building the catalogue that way costs more, and it costs more in the least glamorous way possible: it takes longer. A translated song can be finished in a week. Writing inside the forms means musicians who grew up inside them, arrangements that cannot be assembled from a template, and a great deal of time spent on decisions that no listener will ever be able to name and every listener will feel. It also means giving a permanent frequency to a body of music before you know how many people will find it. A number that belongs to one language cannot be handed to a more popular one later.

The habit that produces the cheap version is not laziness, and it is not disrespect either. It is that one musical grammar spread further than the others and then stopped being audible as a grammar. Four-four time, the diatonic scale, a chord under every melody note and a chorus that resolves: those arrived nearly everywhere with the recording industry, and they now read as neutral rather than as regional. Anything else reads as flavour. So a producer adding a sitar to a worship track believes he is adding India to the song, when the sitar is the one instrument in the room that is not being allowed to do what it does.

The band is arranged to keep that pressure off. Each language holds one permanent frequency, hosted in the language rather than dubbed into it, with its own presenters and its own catalogue, sitting in a regional block beside its neighbours. Nothing on that station has to be justified against what the English-language stations are playing, because it is not competing for the same hour. A frequency of its own is what makes a different musical grammar affordable.
Which brings up the part of this that Western listeners find genuinely difficult.

The objection is a fair one and worth stating properly. Worship music, the argument goes, has to be singable by ordinary people in an ordinary congregation on a Sunday morning; that is its job, and the Western song form is very good at it. Verse, chorus, a hook you have after one hearing, a range that suits untrained voices. All of that is true, and a congregation that cannot sing along has been failed by its musicians. But it proves less than it seems to, because the devotional traditions of the subcontinent are congregational to the bone. A bhajan is sung by whoever is in the room. A kirtan is call and response — the least exclusive musical form there is. Nobody needs training to join the line. The form was never the problem.
The Western song form is not simple. It is familiar, which is a different thing.

In a front room in Ludhiana on a Tuesday night about fifteen people are sitting on the floor with a dholak and a pair of finger cymbals, and they have been on the same line for a long time. Nobody is leading in any formal sense. The tempo has crept up twice. A grandmother is keeping the words going and everyone else comes in underneath her, and a boy of about fifteen who came because there was food afterwards has stopped looking at his phone somewhere around the twentieth repetition, and is now singing it, badly, with his eyes shut. It goes on for another quarter of an hour. When it stops the room is quiet for a moment and then somebody asks about somebody’s knee operation.

That is repetition doing work, and it is the point at which the two traditions genuinely part. What happened to that boy could not have been produced in three verses and a bridge, however well written.

A Western listener hearing thirty repetitions of one line usually reads it as a shortage of material. That reading is not stupid. In the form they know, repetition is a device for reinforcing a hook, and past a certain number of passes it does signal that the writer ran out of things to say. Judged by that standard, a bhajan sounds thin, and a listener who does not stay for the whole of one will hear nothing to correct the impression.

But in the devotional tradition the repetition is not the delivery of the content. It is the mechanism. The line is not being reinforced; it is being worn into somebody, the way water does it, and the thing that happens at the fortieth pass cannot be got at more efficiently because efficiency is not what is being attempted. The boy with his eyes shut did not learn anything new. He was not given information. He was given the same short sentence for long enough that he stopped guarding himself against it.

So the catalogue behind this station was written inside those forms rather than translated into them. Not as a heritage gesture, and not to sound distinctive on a dial: because the forms do something, the something is not decorative, and a song that keeps the words and discards the grammar has kept the smaller half.
All of which is a claim about music until some music is actually playing.

Four kinds of programming share this dial, and knowing that in advance saves a certain amount of confusion. Most of the band is music: worship, gospel, hymns, country, and a great deal that does not sit neatly in any of those. Alongside it runs teaching and prayer, where the Word gets opened and worked through rather than sung. There is family programming, meaning simply that you can leave it on in a room with children in it. And the international block holds a frequency per language, presented by people who speak it, with more numbers assigned and still in build behind the ones already sounding.

So start at HM 332.10 — Inspire India. Start there whether or not you have any Hindi at all, and give it longer than you would normally give a station, because the first four minutes are the least representative four minutes on this band. A melody will go somewhere you did not expect and come back by a route you could not have predicted. A line will come round again, and again, and your instinct will be that the song is stuck. Stay with that one. Somewhere past the point where you would have skipped it, you will notice you are no longer waiting for it to change, and that is the whole argument arriving without a word of explanation.

Nothing needs installing. There is no app, no download and no card to hand over. Open kJubilee.com on the nearest phone or laptop and press play; it was built deliberately for cheap handsets and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually own. Put the page on your home screen if you want it nearer, and it opens like anything else there. Make yourself an account while you are at it, too. Your favourites then travel with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how the band works out which frequencies people keep reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an education in musicology. You do not need to know what a raga is, and you certainly do not need to like the first song. Put HM 332.10 on this evening while you are cooking or driving and leave it running past the point where you would ordinarily reach for the dial. The tradition has never asked anybody to understand it first. It has only ever asked for the same line, a few more times than seems reasonable.
